tutorial.create.0: Tip: use realistic ranges. Many long-term equity assumptions are 5–9% growth and 1–3% inflation. Higher risk or market influence will increase volatility and drawdowns.
tutorial.create.1: Give your simulation a clear name (example: “ETF plan 10 years”, “High risk test”). A good name helps you remember what you were testing and compare scenarios later.
tutorial.create.1b: Classic runs with automatic monthly logic. Hands‑on mode opens a portfolio lab where you can buy/sell and learn the basics of trades and cash balance. You can switch modes later on the run page.
tutorial.create.2: Initial Investment is your starting balance at month 0. Think of it as the money you already have invested today.
tutorial.create.3: Monthly Contribution is how much you invest every month. In real life, consistent contributions often matter more than trying to time the market.
tutorial.create.4: Annual Growth Rate is your long‑term expected return (percent per year). This is an average assumption; real markets move up and down around that average.
tutorial.create.5: Inflation Rate is the yearly increase in prices. The simulator uses it to show “real value”, so you learn the difference between account balance and purchasing power.
tutorial.create.6: Risk Appetite (0–100%) controls how strong the month‑to‑month swings can be. Higher risk means bigger ups and downs and deeper drawdowns.
tutorial.create.7: Market Influence (0–100%) controls how much the simulation reacts to external market shocks. Higher influence makes outcomes more chaotic (more realistic), especially in volatile regimes.
tutorial.create.8: Click Create to save the scenario. After creating, open it and use Step mode first—watch how each month affects contributions, growth, drawdown, and inflation-adjusted value.
tutorial.dashboard.0: You’ll build intuition by running a scenario, stepping month-by-month, and comparing nominal value (account balance) vs real value (purchasing power after inflation).
tutorial.dashboard.1: Welcome! This tutorial will teach you how the investment simulator works and how to use it for learning. You will create a scenario, run it month-by-month, and compare nominal value (money amount) vs real value (purchasing power after inflation).
tutorial.dashboard.2: This is your simulations list. Each row is one saved scenario. Use it to open a simulation and continue experimenting, or edit/delete a scenario you no longer need.
tutorial.dashboard.2b: Each card summarizes one simulation: the name, latest value, gain, and progress (current day vs total). Long names and big numbers are truncated so the grid stays aligned.
tutorial.dashboard.2c: Use Run to open the simulation and start stepping/running. Use Edit to change the scenario inputs (starting amount, contributions, assumptions).
tutorial.dashboard.3: Create a new simulation here. You’ll set a starting amount, monthly contributions, and assumptions (expected growth, inflation, risk and market influence). Then you’ll run it and learn how outcomes change.
tutorial.dashboard.4: Open a simulation to run it month-by-month. If you don’t have one yet, create your first simulation first.
tutorial.show.0: This page has three areas: controls on the left (hover the narrow strip to open), the chart in the center, and a summary on the right. Keep the chart visible while you change settings.
tutorial.show.1: This is your saved simulation. You can step day-by-day to learn, or run the full timeline. The goal is to see how contributions, returns, drawdowns, and inflation work together—not to predict real markets.
tutorial.show.10: The big number above the chart is portfolio value at the current step. Green ↑ or red ↓ under the KPIs in the right column shows change since the previous step.
tutorial.show.14: The right column updates as you Step or Run: money in, gain, real value, max drawdown, and CAGR. Tap the ? next to any label for a short explanation. In hands-on mode you also get allocation and trade stats.
tutorial.show.14b: Simulation Parameters at the bottom is a read-only reminder of what you set when creating the scenario (starting amount, contributions, growth, inflation, risk). To change them, use Edit on the toolbar.
tutorial.show.15: Exercise: set Duration to 3650 days, pick Stress test, then press Step about 30 times. Watch max drawdown and real value in the summary. Then Run to the end and compare portfolio value vs total contributed.
tutorial.show.1b: Run, Pause, Step, Reset, and Save sit on the top bar next to the status badge. Step is best for learning; Run watches the full path; Save only when you want to keep results on the server.
tutorial.show.1c: Auto mode runs the model for you each step. Hands-on mode lets you buy and sell in a practice desk; use Step after trades to move time forward. You can switch anytime.
tutorial.show.2: Hover or focus the left edge (gear strip) to open Simulation Controls. Drag the splitter beside it to give the chart more room—the summary column on the right always stays visible.
tutorial.show.3: Duration is in days. 365 days ≈ one year; 3650 ≈ ten years. Longer runs show compounding and recovery after dips more clearly than a very short run.
tutorial.show.4: Speed is seconds per step while Run is active. It does not change the math—only how fast the timeline plays on screen.
tutorial.show.5: Market Regime changes the mood of returns (steady, bullish, defensive, choppy, stress test). Your scenario inputs stay the same—only the path pattern changes. Try the same setup under two regimes and compare drawdowns.
tutorial.show.5b: Second scenario draws another line on the chart: extra monthly contributions, or the same returns in reverse order (sequence-of-returns risk). Use it to compare choices, not to forecast.
tutorial.show.6: Step moves one day forward—use it to see each change. Run plays the rest automatically in Auto mode. In Hands-on, trade first, then Step; Run is hidden so you control the pace.
tutorial.show.8: Save stores a snapshot and history on the server only when you press it. Use it after a run you want to keep or compare later.
tutorial.show.9: Green is portfolio value, purple is total you put in (break-even vs profit), orange is inflation-adjusted real value. Optional lines show a second scenario. Use the range buttons (All, 12m, …) to zoom the view.
